{{Short description|Variant of the notion of the center of a monoid, group, or ring to a category}}
{{Use American English|date=March 2021}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=March 2021}}

In [[category theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], the '''center''' (or '''Drinfeld center''', after Soviet-American mathematician [[Vladimir Drinfeld]]) is a variant of the notion of the [[Center (algebra)|center]] of a monoid, group, or ring to a category.

==Definition==

The center of a [[monoidal category]] <math>\mathcal{C} = (\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)</math>, denoted <math>\mathcal{Z(C)}</math>, is the category whose objects are pairs <math>(A,u)</math> consisting of an object <math>A</math> of <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and an isomorphism <math>u_X:A \otimes X \rightarrow X \otimes A</math> which is [[natural isomorphism|natural]] in <math>X</math> satisfying
: <math>u_{X \otimes Y} = (1 \otimes u_Y)(u_X \otimes 1)</math>

and

: <math>u_I = 1_A</math> (this is actually a consequence of the first axiom).{{sfn|Majid|1991}}

An arrow from <math>(A,u)</math> to <math>(B,v)</math> in <math>\mathcal{Z(C)}</math> consists of an arrow <math>f\colon A \rightarrow B</math> in <math>\mathcal{C}</math> such that

:<math>v_X (f \otimes 1_X) = (1_X \otimes f) u_X</math>.
This definition of the center appears in {{harvtxt|Joyal|Street|1991}}. Equivalently, the center may be defined as

:<math>\mathcal Z(\mathcal C) = \mathrm{End}_{\mathcal C \otimes \mathcal C^{op}}(\mathcal C),</math>

i.e., the endofunctors of <math>\mathcal C</math> which are compatible with the left and right action of <math>\mathcal C</math> on itself given by the tensor product.

===Braiding===

The category <math>\mathcal{Z(C)}</math> becomes a [[braided monoidal category]] with the tensor product on objects defined as

:<math>(A,u) \otimes (B,v) = (A \otimes B,w)</math>

where <math>w_X = (u_X \otimes 1)(1 \otimes v_X)</math>, and the obvious braiding.

===Higher categorical version===

The categorical center is particularly useful in the context of higher categories. This is illustrated by the following example: the center of the ([[abelian category|abelian]]) category <math>\mathrm{Mod}_R</math> of <math>R</math>-modules, for a [[commutative ring]] <math>R</math>, is <math>\mathrm{Mod}_R</math> again. The center of a monoidal [[Infinity category|∞-category]] <math>\mathcal C</math> can be defined, analogously to the above, as
:<math>Z(\mathcal C) := \mathrm{End}_{\mathcal C \otimes \mathcal C^{op}}(\mathcal C)</math>.
Now, in contrast to the above, the center of the derived category of <math>R</math>-modules (regarded as an ∞-category) is given by the derived category of modules over the cochain complex encoding the [[Hochschild cohomology]], a complex whose degree 0 term is <math>R</math> (as in the abelian situation above), but includes higher terms such as <math>\mathrm{Hom}(R, R)</math> ([[derived functor|derived]] Hom).<ref>{{harvtxt|Ben-Zvi|Francis|Nadler|2010|loc=Remark 1.5}}</ref>

The notion of a center in this generality is developed by {{harvtxt|Lurie|2017|loc=§5.3.1}}. Extending the above-mentioned braiding on the center of an ordinary monoidal category, the center of a monoidal ∞-category becomes an <math>E_2</math>-monoidal category. More generally, the center of a <math>E_k</math>-monoidal category is an algebra object in <math>E_k</math>-monoidal categories and therefore, by [[Dunn additivity]], an <math>E_{k+1}</math>-monoidal category.

==Examples==

{{harvtxt|Hinich|2007}} has shown that the Drinfeld center of the category of sheaves on an [[orbifold]] ''X'' is  the category of sheaves on the [[inertia orbifold]] of ''X''. For ''X'' being the [[classifying space]] of a finite group ''G'', the inertia orbifold is the stack quotient ''G''/''G'', where ''G'' acts on itself by conjugation. For this special case, Hinich's result specializes to the assertion that the center of the category of [[group representation|''G''-representations]] (with respect to some ground field ''k'') is equivalent to the category consisting of ''G''-graded ''k''-vector spaces, i.e., objects of the form
:<math>\bigoplus_{g \in G} V_g</math>
for some ''k''-vector spaces, together with ''G''-equivariant morphisms, where ''G'' acts on itself by conjugation.

In the same vein, {{harvtxt|Ben-Zvi|Francis|Nadler|2010}} have shown that Drinfeld center of the derived category of quasi-coherent sheaves on a perfect stack ''X'' is the derived category of sheaves on the loop stack of ''X''.

==Related notions==

===Centers of monoid objects===
The [[center of a group|center of a monoid]] and the Drinfeld center of a monoidal category are both instances of the following more general concept. Given a monoidal category <math>\mathcal C</math> and a [[monoid object]] <math>A</math> in <math>\mathcal C</math>, the center of <math>A</math> is defined as

:<math>Z(A) = \mathrm{End}_{A \otimes A^{\mathrm{op}}}(A).</math>

For <math>\mathcal C</math> being the category of sets (with the usual cartesian product), a monoid object is simply a monoid, and <math>Z(A)</math> is the center of the monoid. Similarly, if <math>\mathcal C</math> is the category of abelian groups, monoid objects are rings, and the above recovers the [[center (ring theory)|center of a ring]]. Finally, if <math>\mathcal C</math> is the [[category of categories]], with the product as the monoidal operation, monoid objects in <math>\mathcal C</math> are monoidal categories, and the above recovers the Drinfeld center.

===Categorical trace===
The categorical trace of a monoidal category (or monoidal ∞-category) is defined as 
:<math>Tr(C) := C \otimes_{C \otimes C^{op}} C.</math>
The concept is being widely applied, for example in {{harvtxt|Zhu|2018}}.
